title: In the old age: opening of the dark lady sonnets
short: The first of the sonnets (127-152) about the poet's dark-haired, dark-eyed mistress, opening on a paradox about the word 'fair'.
body: 'In the old age' means in former times. 'Fair' meant both beautiful and light-complexioned, so in conventional terms 'black' could not be 'fair'. The sonnet argues that the fashion has changed: because cosmetics have made true fair beauty indistinguishable from false, blackness now inherits beauty's name. The identity of the dark lady (if any real woman lies behind her) is unknown; candidates such as Emilia Lanier or Mary Fitton are speculative. The paradox of a black beauty also appears in Love's Labour's Lost and in Sidney's Astrophil and Stella 7.

sources.cite: Katherine Duncan-Jones, ed., Shakespeare's Sonnets, Arden Shakespeare Third Series (1997; rev. 2010), note on Sonnet 127, headnote

title: beauty's successive heir
short: Black is now the lawful heir in succession to beauty, inheriting its name; the image is of royal or legal inheritance.
body: 'Successive' means coming by right of succession, so that, as Tyler's note puts it, beauty's esteem passes to black. The image makes beauty a dynasty in which black has succeeded to the title. Its opposite is the 'bastard shame' of line 4: true beauty is now slandered as illegitimate because counterfeit beauty has usurped its place. The language of succession would have had topical force in the years of Elizabeth's childless reign, though the sonnet's date is uncertain.

anchor: beauty slander'd with a bastard shame
title: bastard shame
short: Real fair beauty is slandered as illegitimate, since so many 'fair' faces are now painted counterfeits.
body: A 'bastard' is an illegitimate child, and figuratively anything spurious or counterfeit. Because cosmetics have made fair complexions suspect, natural fairness is slandered with the shame of being a bastard, i.e. a fake. Tyler's note sees the shame as the product of art, which falsely claims to rival Nature. The language of legitimacy continues the dynastic image of line 3, and the rhyme 'name / shame' puts beauty's title and its disgrace side by side.

title: each hand hath put on Nature's power
short: Everyone has taken on Nature's prerogative of creating beauty, by painting their faces.
body: 'Each hand' is every hand that applies cosmetics; to 'put on' Nature's power is to usurp it, as one puts on a garment or a role. Giving beauty was Nature's prerogative. The attack on face-painting is a frequent topic in the period's sermons and satires, and in Shakespeare (Hamlet to Ophelia: 'God hath given you one face, and you make yourselves another', 3.1).

title: Fairing the foul
short: Making the ugly look beautiful, and making dark complexions look light, with a false face borrowed from art.
body: 'Fairing' is a verb formed from 'fair': making fair, both in the sense of beautifying and of whitening the skin with ceruse (white lead) and other cosmetics. 'Foul' is the antonym of 'fair' in both senses: ugly and dark. 'Art's false borrowed face' is the cosmetic mask, and 'borrowed' may also suggest wigs made of other people's hair, attacked in Sonnet 68.

title: Sweet beauty hath no name, no holy bower
short: True beauty has lost its name and its sacred dwelling place; it is profaned or lives in disgrace.
body: A 'bower' is a dwelling or inner chamber, here a shrine where beauty might be honoured as a deity. Beauty is 'profan'd' (desecrated, from Latin profanus, outside the temple) by counterfeits. The Quarto spells 'boure'. 'If not lives in disgrace' means 'if it does not (merely) live in disgrace'. The religious language anticipates the mourning of the third quatrain. The line's two negatives ('no name, no holy bower') stress beauty's dispossession.

anchor: my mistress' eyes are raven black
title: my mistress' eyes are raven black
short: The mistress's eyes are glossy black like a raven's; the description is the turn ('Therefore') to the poet's own lady.
body: The 'Therefore' at line 9 marks the turn from general argument to the particular mistress. Raven black is the deepest gloss-black. Petrarchan convention required golden hair and bright eyes, so the dark mistress is an anti-Petrarchan figure (compare Sonnet 130, 'My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun'). Sidney had praised Stella's black eyes, explaining that Nature dressed them in mourning (Astrophil and Stella 7), the conceit Shakespeare reworks here.

title: Her eyes so suited
short: 'Suited' means dressed (in black); because 'eyes' repeats line 9, some editors emend to 'brows' or 'hairs'.
body: The Quarto reads 'Her eyes so suted', and the archive keeps it. The repetition of 'eyes' from the line before has struck many editors as a compositor's error, and nineteenth-century and later editors proposed 'brows' or 'hairs'. A strong support for 'brows' is Berowne's speech in Love's Labour's Lost 4.3: 'O, if in black my lady's brows be deck'd, / It mourns that painting and usurping hair / Should ravish doters with a false aspect'. Others, including the Folger text, keep 'eyes', reading the repetition as emphatic. The note reproduced on Shakespeare Online calls the sense 'clothed' for 'suited' questionable.

title: they mourners seem
short: The black eyes look like mourners dressed in black, grieving for those who use cosmetics to slander creation.
body: Black was the colour of mourning dress. The eyes seem to mourn 'At such who, not born fair, no beauty lack' (people who, though not naturally beautiful, are not without beauty, because they paint), 'Sland'ring creation with a false esteem' (defaming God's or Nature's work by a counterfeit reputation for beauty). The conceit goes back to Sidney's Astrophil and Stella 7, where Stella's black eyes are said to wear mourning.

title: so they mourn becoming of their woe
short: The eyes mourn so gracefully, their grief suiting them so well, that everyone says beauty ought to look like this.
body: 'Becoming of' means gracing or suiting: the mourning becomes them, they look beautiful in it. The couplet completes the paradox of line 1: black, which once could not be called fair, is now the very standard of beauty ('beauty should look so'). Vendler notes the poem's wit in turning fashion into argument. The paradox will be darkened in later sonnets (e.g. 131, 'In nothing art thou black save in thy deeds').
